name: OPTIMAL
aliases: Operations and Pelvic Muscle Training in the Management of Apical Support Loss
question: Does uterosacral ligament suspension or sacrospinous ligament fixation give better results after vaginal apical prolapse repair, and does perioperative behavioral therapy with pelvic floor muscle training improve them?

design.blinding: Participants masked to surgical assignment; surgeons masked to behavioral assignment; outcome assessors masked to both
design.population: 374 women with stage 2–4 apical or uterine prolapse, bulge symptoms and objectively demonstrated stress urinary incontinence who were having vaginal surgery with a retropubic midurethral sling at 9 US centers.
design.description: Multicenter, masked, 2×2 factorial randomized superiority trial
design.locator: Author manuscript PDF pp3–9 (abstract, Methods, Results), Table 1 pp17–20; behavioral arms BPMT n=186 versus usual care n=188 (second randomization)

verdictNote: Neither suspension was superior at 2 years; behavioral therapy added no benefit; 5-year failure estimates did not differ significantly.
takeaway: In women having vaginal apical prolapse repair with a midurethral sling, bilateral uterosacral ligament suspension and unilateral sacrospinous ligament fixation had similar 2-year composite surgical success (64.5% versus 63.1%) and serious adverse events; perioperative behavioral therapy with pelvic floor muscle training did not improve outcomes.

reports.label: 2-year randomized report (corrected 2015)
reports.citation: Barber MD, Brubaker L, Burgio KL, et al. Comparison of 2 transvaginal surgical approaches and perioperative behavioral therapy for apical vaginal prolapse: the OPTIMAL randomized trial. *JAMA.* 2014;311(10):1023-1034.
reports.followUp: 24 months; surgical-success data for 304 of 374 randomized women (155 uterosacral, 149 sacrospinous)
reports.followUpLocator: JAMA online corrected full text, Table 3; abstract

results.measure: 2-year composite surgical success (apical descent no more than one-third of vaginal length, no anterior or posterior wall beyond the hymen, no bothersome bulge, no retreatment); corrected analysis
results.note: Adjusted odds ratio, uterosacral versus sacrospinous. Unadjusted difference 1.4 percentage points (95% CI −9.4 to 12.2). The study was powered to detect a 15-point difference. Corrected 2015; the PMC author manuscript retains the earlier 93/157 (59.2%) versus 92/152 (60.5%).
results.locator: JAMA online corrected full text, Table 3 (POP-Q-derived outcomes); abstract

results.measure: Adjusted mean change from baseline in Urinary Distress Inventory score (range 0–300) at 6 months: −94.6 with BPMT versus −87.9 with usual care
results.note: Mean difference, BPMT minus usual care. Minimum important difference for the score was 11 points.
results.locator: Author manuscript PDF p9 and Table 4 pp28–29; abstract

results.measure: Adjusted mean change from baseline in Pelvic Organ Prolapse Distress Inventory score (range 0–300) at 24 months: −73.3 with BPMT versus −65.2 with usual care
results.note: Mean difference, BPMT minus usual care.
results.locator: Author manuscript PDF p9 and Table 4 pp28–29; abstract

results.measure: 24-month anatomic failure (apical descent beyond one-third of vaginal length, anterior or posterior wall beyond the hymen, or retreatment): 37/153 (24.2%) with BPMT versus 42/164 (25.6%) with usual care; corrected analysis
results.note: The table row appears under the surgical columns in the online text; the counts are the behavioral comparison.
results.locator: JAMA online corrected full text, Table 3 (POP-Q-derived outcomes)

results.measure: Bothersome vaginal bulge symptoms at 24 months, uterosacral versus sacrospinous
results.locator: JAMA online corrected full text, Table 3 (POP-Q-derived outcomes); author manuscript PDF Table 2 p22

results.measure: Retreatment for prolapse by surgery or pessary at 24 months, uterosacral versus sacrospinous
results.note: Adjusted odds ratio; surgery 5/161 (3.1%) versus 4/155 (2.6%), pessary 5/161 (3.1%) versus 5/155 (3.2%).
results.locator: JAMA online corrected full text, Table 3 (POP-Q-derived outcomes); author manuscript PDF Table 2 p22

results.measure: Apical descent greater than one-third of vaginal length at 24 months, uterosacral versus sacrospinous, within usual care
results.note: Interaction between surgical and behavioral assignment (trial not powered for it). Within the BPMT group the figures were 16.2% versus 12.0% (adjusted OR 1.4, 95% CI 0.6–3.7). Overall apical descent: 16/155 (10.3%) versus 21/152 (13.8%).
results.locator: JAMA online corrected full text, Results and Table 3

harms.label: Serious adverse events
harms.locator: Author manuscript PDF p9 and Table 3 p26; abstract
harms.note: Adjusted OR 0.9 (95% CI 0.5–1.6; P=0.83). Modified Dindo grade III: 15/188 (8.0%) versus 17/186 (9.1%); grade IV: 1 versus 1; one death after uterosacral suspension judged unrelated to surgery.

harms.label: Neurologic pain requiring additional treatment
harms.locator: Author manuscript PDF p9 and Table 3 p25
harms.note: Adjusted OR 0.5 (95% CI 0.2–1.0; P=0.049). Present at the 4–6 week visit in 1 (0.5%) versus 8 (4.3%). Return to the operating room for suture removal: 0 versus 3 (1.6%); nerve block 0 versus 2 (1.1%).

harms.label: Intraoperative ureteral obstruction
harms.note: Treated by suture removal in 5 and stent placement in 1. One further ureteral injury after uterosacral suspension was recognized postoperatively. The Results text gives 5 (3.2%).

harms.label: Bladder injury
harms.note: Of the injuries, 18 (9.6%) versus 18 (9.7%) occurred during midurethral sling placement. Rectal injury 0 versus 1 (0.5%).

harms.label: Vaginal granulation tissue, 6 to 24 months
harms.note: Adjusted OR 1.5 (95% CI 0.8–2.6). Suture exposure 29 (15.4%) versus 32 (17.2%); sling erosion or exposure 3 (1.6%) versus 1 (0.5%).

delivery.label: Apical suspension technique
delivery.note: Both used four sutures (two permanent, two delayed absorbable). Uterine prolapse was treated with vaginal hysterectomy; biologic or synthetic graft for the prolapse repair was not allowed.

delivery.label: Concomitant retropubic midurethral sling
delivery.note: Tension-free vaginal tape. Other concomitant surgery was at the surgeon's discretion.

delivery.label: Randomization of surgical assignment
delivery.value: In the operating room, stratified by surgeon and concomitant hysterectomy; 31 surgeons at 9 sites

delivery.label: Perioperative behavioral therapy
delivery.value: One visit 2–4 weeks before surgery and four visits at 2, 4–6, 8 and 12 weeks after
delivery.note: Individualized pelvic floor muscle training and behavioral strategies for urinary and colorectal symptoms. Self-reported exercise performance in the BPMT group was 93.4% at 6 months and 81.4% at 24 months; 8/188 (4.3%) of usual-care women had supervised therapy outside the study.

reports.label: 5-year extension (E-OPTIMAL)
reports.citation: Jelovsek JE, Barber MD, Brubaker L, et al. Effect of uterosacral ligament suspension vs sacrospinous ligament fixation with or without perioperative behavioral therapy for pelvic organ vaginal prolapse on surgical outcomes and prolapse symptoms at 5 years in the OPTIMAL randomized clinical trial. *JAMA.* 2018;319(15):1554-1565.
reports.followUp: 5 years after surgery; 285 of 309 eligible women enrolled and 244 (86%) completed the extension

results.measure: Estimated surgical failure by year 5 (anatomic failure, bothersome bulge or retreatment; time to event), uterosacral versus sacrospinous
results.note: Adjusted probability difference in percentage points, uterosacral minus sacrospinous. Observed first-failure counts at 5 years: 94/145 (64.8%) versus 104/146 (71.2%). Median time to failure 2.6 versus 1.8 years.

results.measure: Estimated anatomic failure by year 5: 45.6% with BPMT versus 47.2% with usual care
results.note: Adjusted risk difference in percentage points, BPMT minus usual care.

results.measure: Change from baseline in Pelvic Organ Prolapse Distress Inventory score by year 5: −59.4 with BPMT versus −61.8 with usual care
results.note: Adjusted mean difference, BPMT minus usual care.

results.measure: Estimated anatomic failure by year 5, uterosacral versus sacrospinous
results.note: Adjusted probability difference in percentage points.

results.measure: Estimated bothersome bulge symptoms by year 5, uterosacral versus sacrospinous
results.note: Adjusted probability difference in percentage points.

results.measure: Retreatment for prolapse by year 5, uterosacral versus sacrospinous
results.note: Adjusted risk difference in percentage points. Pessary 6.0% versus 4.5%; repeat surgery 10/118 (8.5%) versus 5/110 (4.5%).

results.measure: Change from baseline in Pelvic Organ Prolapse Distress Inventory score at 5 years, uterosacral versus sacrospinous
results.note: Adjusted mean difference. Both groups improved by more than the 11-point minimum important difference.

harms.label: Vaginal granulation tissue by 5 years
harms.note: Adjusted risk difference 10.5 percentage points (95% CI −0.2 to 21.2).

harms.label: Suture exposure by 5 years
harms.note: Adjusted risk difference 0.3 percentage points (95% CI −10.8 to 11.4).

harms.label: Midurethral sling erosion or exposure by 5 years
harms.note: Adjusted risk difference −1.9 percentage points (95% CI −6.2 to 2.4).

harms.label: Repeat prolapse surgery by 5 years
harms.note: Adjusted risk difference 3.9 percentage points (95% CI −2.5 to 10.3). The Results text gives 4.6% for sacrospinous.

delivery.label: Failures that later met the composite success definition (post hoc)
delivery.note: At the last clinic visit without further treatment, although the time-to-event analysis kept them classified as failures. Among the 145 failures based on POP-Q measures, 27% involved the apex only, 34% the anterior or posterior compartment only and 39% both.

delivery.label: Modeled 2-year surgical failure in the extension
delivery.note: Adjusted probabilities (95% CI 35.8–55.5 and 40.6–63.3); a participant who met failure criteria stayed a failure at later time points.

relations.note: Same Pelvic Floor Disorders Network; OPUS randomized a sling in women without stress incontinence having vaginal prolapse surgery; all OPTIMAL women had stress incontinence.
